title: English Vocabulary 3 · Units 35–36
description: Curated B2 vocabulary, patterns and usage contrasts for Internet communication, social media and online privacy, with original examples and Brazilian Portuguese translations.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied textbook for personal study. Vocabulary targets reflect the unit study pages, exercises and answer key, while the example sentences and explanatory notes are independently authored. Original passages, extended exercise text and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Full study and exercise pages, illustrated materials, noun/verb contrasts, common collocations, online-privacy guidance and the corresponding answer key reviewed.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British English IPA is included only where sufficiently confident; longer or uncertain pronunciations are deliberately left blank. No bundled recordings or browser voice validation.
audit.languagePolicy: All fields are in English except Brazilian Portuguese translations under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared the uploaded book study pages, exercises and answer key; authored independent examples and notes; checked translations, structural schema, provenance, uniqueness and conservative audio targets offline. No actual VocabLab import, browser TTS or speech-recognition tests.
audit.limitations: No bundled audio. Real app import and speech playback were not tested. References to specific online services are grounded in this 2017 edition and may be dated.

units.title: Unit 35 — Communications and the Internet
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 35. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Distinguish Internet infrastructure, the Web, browsers, search engines and online access methods.
Use natural phrases for navigating sites, finding information, managing accounts and storing data online.
Describe email, servers, video communication, collaborative websites and virtual activities.
Recognise the usage and opposites of log on, log off, log in and log out, and understand textbook-era technology references.

items.example: The Internet connects people and organisations across the world.
items.note: The worldwide network infrastructure; distinguish it from the World Wide Web, which is a service that uses the Internet.

items.pt: World Wide Web; rede de páginas e sites da web
items.example: The World Wide Web gives readers access to linked online pages.
items.note: Usually shortened to the Web; web pages are one part of the Internet.

items.example: The office computers exchange files over the same network.
items.note: Connected devices that can communicate or exchange information.

items.example: The instructions are on a web page maintained by the university.
items.note: A single page of content on the Web, distinct from an entire website.

items.example: A broadband connection made the video call more reliable.
items.note: An internet connection with relatively high data capacity; contrast with older slow connections.

items.example: Visitors have free internet access in the library.
items.note: Access to is the standard combination for the ability to use a service.

items.example: The guesthouse provides wi-fi in every room.
items.note: A wireless networking technology; do not confuse the wireless network itself with the wider Internet.

items.example: The laptop joined the wireless network without an Ethernet cable.
items.note: Devices communicate through radio rather than a cable for the local connection.

items.example: She likes to browse online libraries for articles.
items.note: To look through information or websites, sometimes without an exact goal.

items.example: Open the browser to read the project documentation.
items.note: Software for accessing and displaying web pages; not the same thing as a search engine.

items.example: Use a search engine to find the official documentation.
items.note: A service that searches indexed online content; a browser is the software used to access it.

items.example: The search tool helped us locate an older report.
items.note: Often used with information, files and places; slightly more formal than find.

items.example: I had to google the meaning of that unfamiliar expression.
items.note: Informal verb formed from a company name; the book uses it as an example of language about searching online.

items.example: He spent half an hour surfing the net after work.
items.note: Informal expression for moving between websites, sometimes without a precise purpose.

items.example: The museum website includes details of its opening hours.
items.note: A collection of related web pages under a common address.

items.example: The main navigation menu is on the home page.
items.note: The introductory or main page of a website.

items.example: Follow the link to download the application form.
items.note: A clickable reference to another page, file or resource.

items.example: The menu makes it easy to navigate the website.
items.note: Find your way around a site or between its pages.

items.example: Read the frequently asked questions before contacting support.
items.note: Often abbreviated FAQ; a list of common questions and their answers.

items.example: The FAQ explains how to reset a forgotten password.
items.note: Initialism for frequently asked questions; read the letters separately.

items.pt: salvar nos favoritos; marcador de página
items.example: Bookmark the course website so you can find it again.
items.note: As a verb, save a shortcut to a website; also a noun for that shortcut.

items.example: You can log on to the portal from the university network.
items.note: Log on to a site or network; opposite log off. Similar to log in in many contexts.

items.example: Remember to log off when using a public computer.
items.note: End a session; opposite log on. Often interchangeable with log out.

items.example: The launch attracted thousands of website hits in its first week.
items.note: In informal textbook usage, hits suggest visits or interest; technically an HTTP hit is not necessarily a unique visitor.

items.example: You can subscribe to the news site for monthly updates.
items.note: Subscribe to a site, channel or service; payment may or may not be required.

items.example: Choose a username that is easy for you to remember.
items.note: An account identifier, often paired with a password.

items.example: Do not share your password with other users.
items.note: A secret used to authenticate access to an account.

items.pt: entrar em uma conta; fazer login
items.example: Log in with your username and password to see your results.
items.note: Use credentials to enter an account or service; opposite log out.

items.pt: sair de uma conta; encerrar o login
items.example: Always log out of your account on shared devices.
items.note: End an authenticated session; also called log off.

items.pt: nuvem; armazenamento e serviços na nuvem
items.example: The team keeps a copy of its documents in the cloud.
items.note: In this context, remote online servers or services, not weather.

items.example: You can store data in the cloud and access it from different devices.
items.note: Store means keep; this collocation emphasises remote storage instead of a local device.

items.example: We usually communicate by email when working with overseas partners.
items.note: Use by email for the method; you can also communicate with someone by email.

items.example: The email attachment contains the meeting agenda.
items.note: A separate file sent together with an email.

items.example: Please attach a file containing your updated CV.
items.note: Attach is the verb; attachment is the noun.

items.example: She sent an e-card to congratulate her cousin.
items.note: An electronic greeting card, typically delivered online rather than by post.

items.example: The server stores the documents used by the team.
items.note: A computer or service that provides information or resources to other computers.

items.example: Contact your internet service provider if the connection keeps failing.
items.note: Often abbreviated ISP; a company that supplies an internet connection or related services.

items.pt: estar fora do ar; estar indisponível
items.example: The company's website was down during the upgrade.
items.note: For a server or service, down means not functioning or unavailable.

items.example: In the original course material, people Skype relatives who live overseas.
items.note: Product-specific verb used in the 2017 textbook to describe online calls; examples of such services change over time.

items.example: I added my new colleague to the contact list.
items.note: A collection of people's contact details or online identities.

items.example: Several colleagues were online when I opened the meeting.
items.note: Describes being connected or available through a digital service.

items.example: She switched on her webcam for the video interview.
items.note: A camera that sends live images through a computer or online service.

items.example: The interactive lesson lets learners choose their own answers.
items.note: Users can participate and influence what appears or happens.

items.example: A social networking site helps users keep in contact with each other.
items.note: Online service centred on connections and shared content between people.

items.example: I keep in touch with former classmates through group chats.
items.note: Fixed expression: keep in touch with someone.

items.example: The project wiki contains setup notes contributed by several engineers.
items.note: A site that allows authorised users to create and edit shared pages.

items.example: Team members can edit content on the internal wiki.
items.note: Edit means change or revise existing information.

items.example: Her travel blog includes photographs and practical advice.
items.note: An online publication with posts, often open to reader comments.

items.example: Readers can comment on each article after signing in.
items.note: The standard pattern is comment on something, not comment something.

items.example: Online gaming allows friends in different countries to play together.
items.note: Playing games through a network, sometimes with other people.

items.example: Virtual reality can make a training simulation feel immersive.
items.note: A computer-generated environment a participant can experience, often using specialist equipment.

sectionsChecked: A: Internet terminology, online access and navigating websites
B: Online communication, services and collaborative sites

units.title: Unit 36 — Social media
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 36. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Social media communication, profiles and privacy
learningObjectives: Use social-media verbs with their typical objects, including post, share, follow, subscribe and update.
Describe profiles, uploaded content, comments, likes, views and notification controls.
Distinguish noun and verb uses of post, like, comment and tag.
Talk clearly about account privacy, public posts, timelines, tags, direct messages and default settings.

items.example: She decided to post a video of her cooking experiment.
items.note: Post is a verb here: put content on a social platform for others to see.

items.example: Several friends shared a post about the charity event.
items.note: Share means pass online content on to other users.

items.example: I received a friend request from someone I met at the conference.
items.note: An invitation to connect on a social network; especially associated with some platforms.

items.example: You can send a friend request before viewing the private photos.
items.note: Verb–noun combination for asking another user to become an online contact.

items.example: I'll update my status after we arrive at the hotel.
items.note: Change a short public or selected-audience message about what you are doing.

items.example: Her status says that she is away this week.
items.note: Information or an update shown on a social-media profile.

items.example: Many viewers subscribe to a channel to receive new videos.
items.note: Subscribe to is the standard pattern; the subscription need not be paid.

items.example: I follow several photographers who share useful tutorials.
items.note: Choose to receive or view someone's public posts or updates.

items.example: The new social media app allows users to exchange photographs.
items.note: An application centred on creating, viewing or sharing social content.

items.example: The magazine published a round-up of useful language-learning apps.
items.note: A short review or summary of several developments or products.

items.example: Her profile describes her interests and recent projects.
items.note: Information about a user on an app or website.

items.example: You need to create a profile before posting photographs.
items.note: A frequent verb–noun combination for starting an account's public identity.

items.pt: enviar uma foto para a plataforma; fazer upload de uma foto
items.example: He uploaded a photo of the new laboratory equipment.
items.note: Upload transfers content from a device to an online service.

items.example: The profile asks for basic information about your interests.
items.note: General facts, such as a name, age or short description.

items.example: The organiser will post an update when the event starts.
items.note: An update is new information; post is the verb used to publish it.

items.example: We share links to useful tutorials in our study group.
items.note: Links give access to other pages, files or online resources.

items.example: Visitors can comment on a profile if the owner allows it.
items.note: Comment takes the preposition on before the content being discussed.

items.pt: avaliar um vídeo; dar uma nota a um vídeo
items.example: Users can rate a video from one to five stars.
items.note: Rate involves giving a score or judgement; do not confuse it with simply viewing content.

items.example: The tutorial received over a thousand views.
items.note: As a noun, a view is a recorded instance of someone watching or accessing content.

items.example: I liked a post about urban photography yesterday.
items.note: Like is a verb describing a positive reaction; it is not the same as rating with stars.

items.example: Her photograph received fifty likes within an hour.
items.note: Like is also a countable noun for the reaction.

items.example: The post explained the new schedule in detail.
items.note: Noun meaning a piece of content published online; compare post a video.

items.example: You can write a comment under the photograph.
items.note: Comment can be a countable noun and a verb: write a comment or comment on a post.

items.example: Her comment was helpful and polite.
items.note: Noun: a comment. Verb: comment on something. Both forms occur in the study-page language help.

items.example: I received a notification when my friend posted a new picture.
items.note: A message telling you that something has happened in an app.

items.example: You can turn off notifications while you are studying.
items.note: Turn off is separable: turn notifications off.

items.example: Avoid posting sensitive personal information on public pages.
items.note: Information about a person, such as their address or date of birth.

items.example: You must create an account before using the members' area.
items.note: A standard combination for registering with an online service.

items.example: Only invited friends can see my private photos.
items.note: Visible to a restricted audience; contrast with public.

items.example: The event information is public, so anyone can read it.
items.note: Accessible to everyone rather than a selected group.

items.example: Review your privacy settings before sharing new pictures.
items.note: Controls that determine who can see or interact with your account content.

items.example: She changed her profile picture after the holiday.
items.note: The image representing a user on a social-media account.

items.pt: linha do tempo; sequência de publicações
items.example: His timeline shows updates from several years ago.
items.note: A chronological display of posts, photos or activity on a profile.

items.example: Please ask before you tag someone in a photo.
items.note: To add a person's name or profile link to a post; pattern tag someone in something.

items.example: She asked me to remove the tag from the picture.
items.note: Noun referring to the marker or linked name added to content.

items.example: You can ask the author to remove a tag you did not approve.
items.note: A useful verb–noun combination when managing identification in posts.

items.example: Please send the address in a direct message, not a public reply.
items.note: A message visible only to the participants in the conversation.

items.example: Send a direct message if you need to discuss the payment details.
items.note: Verb–noun pattern for a private message within a platform.

items.example: I decided to delete an account that I no longer used.
items.note: Permanently remove an online account, subject to the site's deletion process.

items.example: The default setting allows messages from registered users.
items.note: The option applied automatically unless a user changes it.

items.pt: manter algo privado; preservar a privacidade de algo
items.example: I prefer to keep my location private on social platforms.
items.note: Pattern: keep something private, meaning prevent general access to it.

items.example: The educational clip got many views after the workshop.
items.note: A video gets views when people watch it; it does not get uploads.

items.example: The new photograph got more likes than the previous one.
items.note: An idiomatic pairing; contrast likes with views.

sectionsChecked: A: Social media verbs and common patterns
B: App review, reactions, noun–verb alternations and notifications
C: Online privacy, account settings and direct messages
